aiGenerationNote:

screens.title: Game State Management and Simple UI
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what game state is, how to manage it with C# variables inside a central GameManager, and how to show that state to players using Unity's Canvas and TextMeshPro elements. We will walk through the singleton GameManager pattern, methods for adding score and taking damage, and how to wire UI elements like score and health text to script references in the Inspector. You will also see how to pause the game and show Game Over or You Win panels by using a boolean game-over flag, Time. timeScale, and simple panel activation. The practical outcome is a small, testable loop where collecting coins updates score, hazards reduce health, and a restart button reloads the scene. By the end you will be comfortable separating global state from player-specific state, avoiding common errors such as null references or forgetting to include the TextMeshPro namespace, and connecting UI buttons to public methods. Think of this as the backbone that keeps the player's experience consistent and debuggable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus on practical skills you will use to build a basic, reliable game loop. First, you will understand the idea of game state and how it is represented by variables such as integers for score, floats for health, and booleans for flags like game over. Second, you will implement core game logic: updating score on events, reducing health on damage, and checking conditions using if statements to trigger win or game-over behaviors. Third, you will create a Canvas and add TextMeshProUGUI text elements so players see live values like score and health. Fourth, you will wire those UI elements to C# by creating public references in your GameManager script and assigning them in the Inspector. Each skill is essential: variables and logic keep behavior deterministic, while UI bindings make state visible and testable. As you work, you'll practice small, repeatable steps and verify the visible output so debugging is faster and clearer.

screens.title: What is Game State?
screens.narratorSegment: Game state is the set of values that describe everything important about a play session: the player's score, remaining health, which level is active, how many enemies remain, and whether the game is paused or over. Think of state as the single source of truth that determines what can happen next. For example, a score integer increases when a coin is collected; a health float decreases when damaged; a boolean like isGameOver prevents further input and triggers a game-over panel. A clear definition helps you design predictable transitions. A common misconception is treating state as spread across many scripts without coordination — that leads to bugs because no single component knows the full truth. A practical pattern is to centralize global state in a GameManager script and keep player-specific values local. This reduces coupling and makes condition checks straightforward: if playerHealth reaches zero, set isGameOver true, stop input, and display the Game Over UI. As a takeaway, always ask: what values define whether the player can keep interacting? Those values are your game state. What is Game State? means game state is the authoritative set of variables that determine how the game behaves at any moment.. In practical terms, the collection of values that describe the current play session. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is Game State?
Game State — core idea
Everything needed to understand the current session.
Example components
  • score: integer that increments when collecting items
  • playerHealth: float that decreases on damage
  • isGameOver: boolean that gates input and triggers panels
Why centralize?
Centralizing global values prevents scattered logic, making checks and transitions predictable and easier to debug.
Common mistake
Putting too much global logic inside the player script causes tight coupling and harder-to-read code. Use GameManager for global concerns.
Key Takeaway

Identify the small set of variables that fully describe whether gameplay should continue and manage them centrally.

Analogy
State as a scoreboard
Like a single scoreboard that tells referees what to do — who scored, time left, and whether the game is paused — game state drives decisions in your code. Keep it authoritative.
Check your understanding
What variable would you set when health reaches zero to stop player input?
Why is it problematic to update UI directly from several different scripts?

screens.title: Variables That Store State
screens.narratorSegment: State variables are the simplest building blocks of game state. Use an integer for quantities like score because points are whole numbers. Use a float for measures that may need fractional values like health or timers. Use a boolean to represent binary conditions such as isGameOver or isPaused. In C#, that translates to statements like int score; float playerHealth; bool isGameOver;. Declaring these in a single script — typically the GameManager — makes them easy to access and reason about. A concrete example: when a coin is collected, call a method AddScore that increases the score integer by a fixed amount; when an enemy hits the player, call TakeDamage to subtract from playerHealth, and check if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero to set isGameOver to true. A common misconception is choosing the wrong type — using float where an int makes sense can complicate comparisons. The practical step-by-step is: declare your variables, initialize them in Start, update them in event handlers, and then trigger UI updates so players see the change. This keeps logic predictable and testable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Variables That Store State
Common state variables
Use clear names and initialize them in Start or Awake so their values are predictable when play begins.
Score — int
Whole-number point totals, increment when collecting items.
Health — float
Allows fractional damage and smooth bars when mapped to an Image fillAmount.
isGameOver — bool
Stops input and toggles end screens when true.
Key Takeaway

Pick the simplest type that expresses the value and initialize it early to avoid unexpected null or default behavior.

Code example
// Declarations inside GameManager
public int score = 0;
public float playerHealth = 100f;
public bool isGameOver = false;

// Initialization
void Start()
{
  UpdateScoreUI();
  UpdateHealthUI();
  isGameOver = false;
}
Misconception
Avoid scattering these variables across unrelated scripts. Centralize global values so logic checks are simple and consistent.

screens.title: GameManager Singleton Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A GameManager is a script whose responsibility is to manage global game state and coordinate UI and scene-level behavior. The singleton pattern is commonly used: it ensures there is a single instance accessible from any other script via a static property like Instance. In Awake you check if Instance already exists and destroy duplicates, otherwise assign Instance to this and optionally call DontDestroyOnLoad to persist it between scenes. This pattern simplifies calls such as GameManager. Instance. AddScore from player or coin scripts. A concrete example is implementing Awake to guard against duplicates and Start to initialize the UI. A common pitfall is making public static fields mutable without access control; favor methods to change state. Also avoid storing per-player transient data in the singleton; keep per-player health on the player component. The takeaway is that a well-written GameManager makes state access explicit and reduces reference wiring in many small scripts. GameManager Singleton Pattern means use a singleton gamemanager to centralize global state and provide a simple api for other scripts to call.. In practical terms, one authoritative gamemanager for global state and coordination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › GameManager Singleton
Singleton pattern
Ensure a single, globally available GameManager instance and prevent accidental duplicates.
Awake guard
If Instance exists and is not this, destroy the duplicate. Otherwise set Instance and optionally call DontDestroyOnLoad.
Public methods only
Expose methods like AddScore and TakeDamage instead of letting other scripts change fields directly.
Separation rule
Keep per-player transient data on the player script and global counters in the manager.
Pro tip

When testing, ensure only one GameManager exists in the scene to avoid silent duplicate behavior.

Awake example
void Awake()
{
    if (Instance != null && Instance != this)
    {
        Destroy(gameObject);
    }
    else
    {
        Instance = this;
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }
}
Misconception
Persisting everything with DontDestroyOnLoad can inadvertently carry state between level tests; only persist the manager when you need cross-scene continuity.

screens.title: AddScore and TakeDamage Methods
screens.narratorSegment: AddScore and TakeDamage are the two workhorse methods that change game state in response to gameplay events. AddScore should check whether the game is over before adding points, update the score variable, call UpdateScoreUI, and optionally check for win conditions. TakeDamage should subtract a given amount from playerHealth, clamp the value so it never drops below zero, update the health UI, and call GameOver when health reaches zero. A concrete example is when a coin triggers AddScore: the coin collider calls GameManager. Instance. AddScore with a coin value. Another real example is an enemy collision calling TakeDamage. A common mistake is forgetting the isGameOver guard, which can let score change after the game ends. Use Debug. Log calls to confirm values during play, and update UI only from the GameManager to avoid race conditions. Keep the methods concise and well-documented so they remain the single source of truth for state transitions. AddScore and TakeDamage Methods means write guarded methods that modify variables, update ui, and check end-state conditions in one place.. In practical terms, update state and ui reliably when events occur. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › AddScore & TakeDamage
Methods that change state
Keep checks, updates, UI refresh, and win/lose logic together.
AddScore — responsibilities
  • Return early if isGameOver
  • Increase score variable and UpdateScoreUI()
  • Check collectedCoins vs totalCoinsInScene to WinGame()
TakeDamage — responsibilities
  • Return early if isGameOver
  • Subtract from playerHealth and clamp to zero
  • UpdateHealthUI() and call GameOver() if needed
Key Takeaway

Keep modification and UI refresh together so the displayed state never lags behind the actual state.

Code excerpts
public void AddScore(int amount)
{
    if (isGameOver) return;

    score += amount;
    UpdateScoreUI();
    Debug.Log("Score updated: " + score);

    if (amount > 0 && amount == 10)
    {
        collectedCoins++;
        if (collectedCoins >= totalCoinsInScene)
        {
            WinGame();
        }
    }
}

public void TakeDamage(float amount)
{
    if (isGameOver) return;

    playerHealth -= amount;
    playerHealth = Mathf.Max(0, playerHealth);
    UpdateHealthUI();

    if (playerHealth <= 0)
    {
        GameOver();
    }
}

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Canvas & TextMeshProUGUI
Create and configure UI
Set up Canvas, add TextMeshPro elements, and import TextMeshPro resources when prompted.
Canvas settings
Use Screen Space - Overlay and set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size for consistent layout.
Panels and initial state
Create GameOverPanel and GameWinPanel and disable them in the Inspector until needed.
Key Takeaway

TextMeshProUGUI is preferred for readable, high-quality text. Always import its resources when prompted.

Inspector mapping example
// At top of GameManager.cs
using TMPro; // Required for TextMeshProUGUI

[Header("UI References")]
public TextMeshProUGUI scoreText;
public TextMeshProUGUI healthText;
public GameObject gameOverPanel;
public GameObject gameWinPanel;

// In Start()
gameOverPanel.SetActive(false);
gameWinPanel.SetActive(false);
If the fields are null at runtime, Unity will show a NullReferenceException. Assign the UI objects in the Inspector to avoid this.

screens.title: Updating UI from Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Updating UI from a script requires two steps. First, create a public TextMeshProUGUI field in your GameManager and include using TMPro at the top of the file. Second, assign the actual UI GameObject from the Hierarchy into that field in the Inspector by dragging the ScoreText onto the script slot. Once assigned, whenever your score or health variables change, call UpdateScoreUI or UpdateHealthUI to set the text property of the TextMeshProUGUI component. For example, UpdateScoreUI can set scoreText. text = "Score: " + score. ToString();. For health bars you may instead set an Image's fillAmount based on playerHealth divided by maxHealth. A common error is forgetting to add using TMPro, which makes TextMeshProUGUI undefined and leads to compile errors, or leaving Inspector references unassigned, which triggers NullReferenceExceptions at runtime. As a workflow, change the value in code, hit play, and watch the UI update; if it doesn't, inspect the console for null or missing reference errors and trace back to the Inspector assignments. Updating UI from Scripts means declare textmeshprougui fields, assign them in the inspector, and update their text property whenever state changes.. In practical terms, connect textmeshprougui references and refresh text when state changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Updating UI from Scripts
Inspector binding and updates
Assign references, then update UI whenever your variables change.
Two-step workflow
  1. Declare public TextMeshProUGUI fields and add using TMPro;
  2. Drag the UI GameObjects into the Inspector fields;
  3. Call UpdateScoreUI() after changing score.
Example text update
scoreText.text = "Score: " + score.ToString();
Common mistake

NullReferenceException at UpdateScoreUI usually means the Inspector field was not assigned. Reassign the UI object to the script slot.

UpdateScoreUI example
void UpdateScoreUI()
{
    if (scoreText != null)
    {
        scoreText.text = "Score: " + score.ToString();
    }
}

{
    if (healthText != null)
    {
        healthText.text = "Health: " + playerHealth.ToString("F0");

screens.title: Game Over vs You Win
screens.narratorSegment: Game Over and You Win are two end states that share handling patterns but differ in triggers and messaging. Both set isGameOver true, pause gameplay using Time. timeScale set to zero, and activate a UI panel. The difference lies in the trigger: Game Over occurs when playerHealth reaches zero or a fail condition is met; You Win is triggered when score or collected items meet a target. For instance, collect all coins and call WinGame; take damage until health is zero and call GameOver. Both methods should prevent further score changes and show the appropriate panel. A common misconception is to forget to unpause the game before reloading the scene; RestartGame should set Time. timeScale back to one to resume physics and updates. Also consider cursor visibility and lock state: when pausing for UI, unlock and show the cursor so the player can click Restart. The takeaway is to treat end states consistently: set flags, update UI, and manage time and input cleanly. Game Over vs You Win means treat win and lose states similarly: mark the state, show the relevant ui, pause time, and restore time on restart.. In practical terms, distinct end states, same handling pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Game Over vs You Win
Compare triggers and handling
Both states use the same cleanup steps but have different triggers and UI text.
Game Over
  • Trigger: playerHealth ≤ 0 or fail condition
  • Action: set isGameOver, show GameOverPanel, Time.timeScale = 0
You Win
  • Trigger: collectedCoins ≥ totalCoinsInScene or score threshold
  • Action: set isGameOver, show GameWinPanel, Time.timeScale = 0
Pro tip

Always restore Time.timeScale to one before reloading a scene to avoid frozen physics after restart.

Example methods
public void GameOver()
{
    if (isGameOver) return;
    isGameOver = true;
    if (gameOverPanel != null) gameOverPanel.SetActive(true);
    Time.timeScale = 0f;
    Cursor.lockState = CursorLockMode.None;
    Cursor.visible = true;
}

public void WinGame()
{
    if (isGameOver) return;
    isGameOver = true;
    if (gameWinPanel != null) gameWinPanel.SetActive(true);
    Time.timeScale = 0f;
}

Event wiring
Make collisions and triggers call the GameManager to keep logic centralized.
Tag and collider rules
Coins should have the Coin tag and be triggers; hazards can be triggers or collide physically as needed.
Null check pitfall
Ensure GameManager exists and Awake ran before other scripts attempt to call Instance methods.
Key Takeaway

Connect event scripts to the manager to keep gameplay changes consistent and centralized.

CoinCollector example
void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
{
    if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
    {
        GameManager.Instance.AddScore(coinValue);
        Destroy(other.gameObject);
    }
    else if (other.CompareTag("Hazard"))
    {
        GameManager.Instance.TakeDamage(damageAmount);
    }
}

void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
{
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
    {
        GameManager.Instance.TakeDamage(damageAmount);
    }
}
Attach this script to the player, set coinValue and damageAmount, and verify tags on scene objects to ensure expected behavior.

screens.narratorSegment: When you test the game loop, follow a short checklist to catch common mistakes quickly. First, verify the GameManager object exists in the scene and that Awake sets Instance. Fifth, press the Restart button and ensure the scene reloads and Time. timeScale returns to one. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what game state is, how to manage it with C# variables inside a central GameManager, and how to show that state to players using Unity's Canvas and TextMeshPro elements. We will walk through the singleton GameManager pattern, methods for adding score and taking damage, and how to wire UI elements like score and health text to script references in the Inspector. You will also see how to pause the game and show Game Over or You Win panels by using a boolean game-over flag, Time. timeScale, and simple panel activation. The practical outcome is a small, testable loop where collecting coins updates score, hazards reduce health, and a restart button reloads the scene. By the end you will be comfortable separating global state from player-specific state, avoiding common errors such as null references or forgetting to include the TextMeshPro namespace, and connecting UI buttons to public methods. Think of this as the backbone that keeps the player's experience consistent and debuggable.

These learning objectives focus on practical skills you will use to build a basic, reliable game loop. First, you will understand the idea of game state and how it is represented by variables such as integers for score, floats for health, and booleans for flags like game over. Second, you will implement core game logic: updating score on events, reducing health on damage, and checking conditions using if statements to trigger win or game-over behaviors. Third, you will create a Canvas and add TextMeshProUGUI text elements so players see live values like score and health. Fourth, you will wire those UI elements to C# by creating public references in your GameManager script and assigning them in the Inspector. Each skill is essential: variables and logic keep behavior deterministic, while UI bindings make state visible and testable. As you work, you'll practice small, repeatable steps and verify the visible output so debugging is faster and clearer.

This second objectives page focuses on application and debugging skills you will use immediately in the Unity Editor. First, you will learn the singleton pattern for a GameManager so other scripts can call shared methods without direct references. Second, you will practice separating global game state from player-local state, keeping the GameManager lean while storing per-player health on the player object. Third, you will wire Restart and Pause functionality using public methods and Button OnClick events. Fourth, you will learn common troubleshooting steps: include the TextMeshPro namespace, ensure Inspector fields are assigned, and verify panels are initially disabled. These skills help you move from a prototype to a resilient loop that is easier to extend and test. Each objective is chosen so your editor work produces visible, testable results in play mode.

Game state is the set of values that describe everything important about a play session: the player's score, remaining health, which level is active, how many enemies remain, and whether the game is paused or over. Think of state as the single source of truth that determines what can happen next. For example, a score integer increases when a coin is collected; a health float decreases when damaged; a boolean like isGameOver prevents further input and triggers a game-over panel. A clear definition helps you design predictable transitions. A common misconception is treating state as spread across many scripts without coordination — that leads to bugs because no single component knows the full truth. A practical pattern is to centralize global state in a GameManager script and keep player-specific values local. This reduces coupling and makes condition checks straightforward: if playerHealth reaches zero, set isGameOver true, stop input, and display the Game Over UI. As a takeaway, always ask: what values define whether the player can keep interacting? Those values are your game state. What is Game State? means game state is the authoritative set of variables that determine how the game behaves at any moment.. In practical terms, the collection of values that describe the current play session. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

State variables are the simplest building blocks of game state. Use an integer for quantities like score because points are whole numbers. Use a float for measures that may need fractional values like health or timers. Use a boolean to represent binary conditions such as isGameOver or isPaused. In C#, that translates to statements like int score; float playerHealth; bool isGameOver;. Declaring these in a single script — typically the GameManager — makes them easy to access and reason about. A concrete example: when a coin is collected, call a method AddScore that increases the score integer by a fixed amount; when an enemy hits the player, call TakeDamage to subtract from playerHealth, and check if playerHealth is less than or equal to zero to set isGameOver to true. A common misconception is choosing the wrong type — using float where an int makes sense can complicate comparisons. The practical step-by-step is: declare your variables, initialize them in Start, update them in event handlers, and then trigger UI updates so players see the change. This keeps logic predictable and testable.

A GameManager is a script whose responsibility is to manage global game state and coordinate UI and scene-level behavior. The singleton pattern is commonly used: it ensures there is a single instance accessible from any other script via a static property like Instance. In Awake you check if Instance already exists and destroy duplicates, otherwise assign Instance to this and optionally call DontDestroyOnLoad to persist it between scenes. This pattern simplifies calls such as GameManager. Instance. AddScore from player or coin scripts. A concrete example is implementing Awake to guard against duplicates and Start to initialize the UI. A common pitfall is making public static fields mutable without access control; favor methods to change state. Also avoid storing per-player transient data in the singleton; keep per-player health on the player component. The takeaway is that a well-written GameManager makes state access explicit and reduces reference wiring in many small scripts. GameManager Singleton Pattern means use a singleton gamemanager to centralize global state and provide a simple api for other scripts to call.. In practical terms, one authoritative gamemanager for global state and coordination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AddScore and TakeDamage are the two workhorse methods that change game state in response to gameplay events. AddScore should check whether the game is over before adding points, update the score variable, call UpdateScoreUI, and optionally check for win conditions. TakeDamage should subtract a given amount from playerHealth, clamp the value so it never drops below zero, update the health UI, and call GameOver when health reaches zero. A concrete example is when a coin triggers AddScore: the coin collider calls GameManager. Instance. AddScore with a coin value. Another real example is an enemy collision calling TakeDamage. A common mistake is forgetting the isGameOver guard, which can let score change after the game ends. Use Debug. Log calls to confirm values during play, and update UI only from the GameManager to avoid race conditions. Keep the methods concise and well-documented so they remain the single source of truth for state transitions. AddScore and TakeDamage Methods means write guarded methods that modify variables, update ui, and check end-state conditions in one place.. In practical terms, update state and ui reliably when events occur. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unity's Canvas is the container for all on-screen UI. Create a Canvas (UI → Canvas) and set its Render Mode to Screen Space - Overlay for a simple HUD. Inside the Canvas add TextMeshPro - Text (UI) elements for ScoreText and HealthText. TextMeshPro is recommended for better rendering and requires the using TMPro namespace in your scripts. When you first add a TextMeshPro component, Unity prompts to import essential resources — accept them. Place ScoreText and HealthText where they are visible during play, typically top-left and top-right. Also create two panels: GameOverPanel and GameWinPanel, each containing a TextMeshPro label and a Restart button. Disable both panels in the Inspector so they appear only when needed. The concrete example is creating ScoreText, assigning it to a public TextMeshProUGUI field in GameManager, and then calling UpdateScoreUI when the score changes. Doing this makes the game's internal state visible immediately to the player. Canvas and TextMeshProUGUI Setup means canvas holds ui; textmeshprougui elements provide high-quality, scriptable text that you assign to gamemanager references.. In practical terms, create ui elements and import textmeshpro resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Updating UI from a script requires two steps. First, create a public TextMeshProUGUI field in your GameManager and include using TMPro at the top of the file. Second, assign the actual UI GameObject from the Hierarchy into that field in the Inspector by dragging the ScoreText onto the script slot. Once assigned, whenever your score or health variables change, call UpdateScoreUI or UpdateHealthUI to set the text property of the TextMeshProUGUI component. For example, UpdateScoreUI can set scoreText. text = "Score: " + score. ToString();. For health bars you may instead set an Image's fillAmount based on playerHealth divided by maxHealth. A common error is forgetting to add using TMPro, which makes TextMeshProUGUI undefined and leads to compile errors, or leaving Inspector references unassigned, which triggers NullReferenceExceptions at runtime.
